stem: A client with retained respiratory secretions is receiving postural drainage as part of an individualized airway-clearance plan. Which description of the technique is accurate?

options.A: Position the client so gravity helps move secretions from targeted lung regions toward larger airways; percussion or vibration and coached breathing or coughing may be added as appropriate.
options.B: Use the same drainage position for each treatment area and rely on gravity alone, because percussion, vibration, and coughing do not contribute to secretion clearance.
options.C: Place the client in the position that produces the strongest cough regardless of the lung region involved, then suppress coughing after treatment so loosened mucus remains mobilized.
options.D: Use postural drainage routinely for respiratory symptoms even when excess secretions are absent, because the technique is selected by diagnosis rather than secretion burden or tolerance.

rationale: Current NCBI StatPearls guidance describes postural drainage as positioning the body so gravity helps drain mucus from specific lung areas toward larger airways. Manual chest physiotherapy may add percussion or vibration to loosen and mobilize mucus, and deep breathing and coughing may be used during or after treatment to help expel loosened secretions. The same source states that airway-clearance technique selection depends on the disease, the client's general health, secretion burden, tolerance, and contraindications. The AARC 2013 airway-clearance guideline likewise defines chest physiotherapy as percussion, vibration, and postural drainage and emphasizes matching therapy to the patient's disease process, ability, preferences, and technique limitations. Therefore A is correct. B ignores segment-specific positioning and complementary techniques, C disregards the targeted lung region and suppresses an important clearance mechanism, and D applies the intervention without a secretion-clearance indication or individualized assessment.
educational_objective: Describe postural drainage as individualized, gravity-assisted positioning for retained secretions that targets specific lung regions and may be combined with percussion, vibration, breathing, and coughing techniques when appropriate.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf, StatPearls; American Association for Respiratory Care (AARC)
source_document_title: Postural Drainage and Vibration; AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Effectiveness of Nonpharmacologic Airway Clearance Therapies in Hospitalized Patients
source_version_date: StatPearls article last updated June 8, 2024 and published in the 2026 StatPearls edition; AARC guideline published 2013 and remains listed on AARC's current guideline resources in 2026
source_locator: StatPearls Postural Drainage and Vibration > Introduction: postural drainage positions the body to use gravity to drain mucus from specific lung areas; vibration uses rhythmic pressure to loosen mucus. > Indications: airway-clearance techniques are used when mucus retention or impaired clearance is present; therapy selection depends on disease and general health; postural drainage should not be used when excess mucus removal is not required or the position cannot be tolerated. > Technique or Treatment > Manual Chest Physiotherapy: different positions facilitate drainage from different lung segments; gravity moves mucus toward larger airways; percussion loosens/mobilizes mucus; deep breathing and coughing may help expel loosened secretions. AARC 2013 guideline > Introduction and airway-clearance table: airway-clearance therapy mobilizes secretions cephalad and facilitates evacuation by coughing; breathing maneuvers, gravity-assisted drainage, manual techniques, and devices may be used; chest physiotherapy includes percussion, vibration, and postural drainage; therapy should be matched to the patient's disease process, ability, preferences, and technique limitations.
source_claim_supported: Postural drainage uses targeted positioning and gravity to move retained mucus toward larger airways; percussion/vibration and breathing/coughing may complement clearance, and technique selection should be individualized rather than routine for all respiratory symptoms.

supporting_sources.document_title: AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Effectiveness of Nonpharmacologic Airway Clearance Therapies in Hospitalized Patients
supporting_sources.version_date: Published 2013; current on AARC guideline resources in 2026
supporting_sources.locator: Introduction: airway-clearance therapy uses physical or mechanical means to mobilize secretions cephalad and facilitate evacuation by coughing; breathing maneuvers, gravity-assisted drainage, manual techniques, and devices may be used. Table of Airway Clearance Therapies: chest physiotherapy includes percussion, vibration, and postural drainage. Therapy-selection paragraph: match therapy to disease process, cognitive ability/preferences, and technique/device limitations.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Chest physiotherapy can combine postural drainage with percussion/vibration, and airway-clearance therapy should be individualized rather than treated as a universal routine.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed pp. 46–47 (PDF pp. 50–51): related activity statement 'Provide pulmonary hygiene (e.g., chest physiotherapy, incentive spirometry)'; related content again lists 'Provide pulmonary hygiene (e.g., chest physiotherapy, incentive spirometry)' and management of impaired ventilation/oxygenation.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — chest physiotherapy/postural drainage for secretion clearance
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four descriptions to remove the uniquely-long keyed response and replace obvious distractors with clinically plausible errors involving non-targeted positioning, suppression of cough, and routine use without a secretion-clearance indication. The item was remapped to Physiological Adaptation because the 2026 NCSBN Test Plan explicitly places pulmonary hygiene and chest physiotherapy there.

audit_findings.stem: PASS — establishes retained secretions and an individualized airway-clearance plan, avoiding the unsupported implication that every respiratory diagnosis requires postural drainage.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects gravity-assisted segment-specific positioning and appropriately conditional use of percussion/vibration and breathing/coughing; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — gravity is central, but drainage positions vary by target lung segment and percussion/vibration/coughing can contribute to clearance.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — cough is useful, but positioning is selected according to the targeted region rather than the position producing the strongest cough, and suppressing cough conflicts with mucus evacuation.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — postural drainage can be useful in selected respiratory disorders, but current guidance ties airway-clearance therapy to retained secretions, clinical status, tolerance, and contraindications rather than respiratory symptoms alone.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that accurately combines targeted gravity-assisted positioning with conditional complementary clearance maneuvers and individualized selection.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B removes segment-specific technique and useful adjuncts, C uses the wrong positioning criterion and suppresses cough, and D universalizes treatment without an airway-clearance indication.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all four alternatives are closely matched in length and specificity; the keyed answer is no longer uniquely long.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Physiological Adaptation explicitly lists pulmonary hygiene including chest physiotherapy.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether percussion/vibration must always be part of postural drainage or whether diagnosis alone can justify treatment. Current sources describe manual techniques as optional components and emphasize individualized selection based on secretion retention, clinical state, tolerance, and contraindications; A preserves that conditionality and remains uniquely correct.
